title: The Soviet Union invades eastern Poland
subtitle: The second invasion and the closing roads
body:
Before dawn on September 17, 1939, Polish ambassador Wacław Grzybowski was summoned to hear that the state he represented no longer existed. The Soviet note asserted that Poland’s government had collapsed, its treaties had lost their force and Ukrainians and Belarusians required protection. Grzybowski refused to accept it. Warsaw was still resisting Germany; Polish armies were still fighting; the government had not yet left the country. That morning, the Red Army was crossing the frontier to occupy territory whose conquest Moscow had presented as the consequence of an accomplished collapse. The note’s sequence was convenient for the invader. By declaring Polish authority extinguished, Moscow claimed release from its obligations to Poland and represented military entry as protection of an abandoned population. The American ambassador’s report preserves the argument as issued that morning. Soviet orders and private exchanges with Germany tell a different story: the advance and its public justification had been prepared while Poland’s armed resistance continued. [1] [2] For Polish soldiers and civilians, the practical question was more immediate. Much of the country was already exposed to the German offensive described in the [previous study](/articles/german-invasion-poland-1939-09-01). The east contained military depots, replacement units, roads toward neutral neighbors and people who had fled the fighting farther west. Soviet intervention brought another army into this remaining space. It threatened the possibility of regrouping, but also the simpler hope that continuing eastward would lead a family away from the war. The [August agreement](/articles/molotov-ribbentrop-pact-1939-08-23) supplied the diplomatic framework for partition. The decisions of September gave it military force. Berlin and Moscow discussed timing, military contacts and the language of their public explanations; Polish commanders faced the second attack with damaged communications and formations already dispersed by the first. Their decisions about resistance, escape and surrender determine the human course of this study, which follows the invasion into the fighting at Grodno and Lwów and the last resistance of the Border Protection Corps at Wytyczno on October 1.

A pretext prepared in advance

Moscow’s public explanation was being discussed with Germany a week before Soviet troops crossed the border. On September 10, Foreign Commissar Vyacheslav Molotov told the German ambassador, Friedrich-Werner von der Schulenburg, that the speed of Germany’s advance had surprised the Soviet leadership. Military preparations had to be accelerated. Molotov also explained the political story he intended to tell: Poland was collapsing, and the Soviet Union must protect Ukrainians and Belarusians threatened by Germany. According to Schulenburg’s report, Molotov considered that explanation necessary to keep the intervention from appearing aggressive. [3] Molotov also worried that a German–Polish armistice would spoil the explanation: Soviet entry after a cease-fire would look like the beginning of a new war. For him, the continuing German attack created an opportunity and a deadline. The protective formula was being constructed while military preparations were accelerated. Schulenburg’s report connects those two processes directly, before the Soviet government publicly announced that necessity had left it no alternative. On September 14, Molotov said that military action could begin sooner than previously expected, but he wanted to know when Warsaw would fall. The capital’s capture would strengthen the claim that Poland had ceased to function. Soviet newspapers were already preparing the political explanation. Warsaw, however, continued to resist. The invasion would go ahead without the event that Moscow had hoped to use as its most convincing evidence. [4] Berlin wanted Soviet intervention, but objected to being cast as the danger from which the Red Army was rescuing its neighbors. On September 15, Joachim von Ribbentrop instructed Schulenburg to explain that such language would present the two governments as enemies. His message also pressed for the date and hour of Soviet entry and for arrangements between military representatives. Germany’s interest was practical as well as political: Soviet action could spare German forces the task of pursuing the remaining Polish armies all the way toward the Soviet frontier. [5] At about two in the morning on September 17, Stalin received Schulenburg with Molotov and Defense Commissar Kliment Voroshilov present. He announced that Soviet forces would cross that morning. The discussion included a proposed limit for German aircraft along the Białystok–Brest–Lwów line, intended to reduce the danger of clashes between the advancing armies. Stalin also read the diplomatic note intended for Poland and, according to the German report, altered three passages after Schulenburg objected. The telegram does not preserve the discarded wording; it does establish that Germany had an opportunity to influence the explanation before Poland received it. [6]

The production of an official explanation

Stalin revised the joint communiqué

Hilger’s memorandum of September 18 records a second process of revision, separate from the earlier changes to the note addressed to Poland. The German draft proposed a new territorial and economic order. Stalin judged its language excessively candid and supplied another text, whose publication required Berlin’s assent. The two drafts survive as enclosures. Their differences allow the historian to examine the preparation of the public explanation, while Hilger’s account remains a German diplomatic record rather than an independent transcript of Stalin’s intentions.

[7]
The armies would remain under separate commands, but the governments were arranging how to advance without obstructing each other. Advance notice, military representatives and restrictions intended to avoid aerial clashes made cooperation practical. Poland had no representative in these conversations. Its forces were the opponents to be defeated, and its territory the ground on which the two invaders were negotiating their respective freedom of action.

Orders, formations and directions

The military instructions make the planning visible. Directives 16633 and 16634, issued on September 14 over the names of Voroshilov and Chief of the General Staff Boris Shaposhnikov, ordered secret concentration, readiness by the end of September 16 and an offensive across the frontier at dawn on the 17th. They assigned commanders, forces, successive objectives and deadlines. Their language concerned defeating opposing troops. These were orders for an invasion, already prepared before the protective explanation was delivered. [8] [9] Mikhail Kovalyov commanded the Byelorussian Front in the north and Semyon Timoshenko the Ukrainian Front in the south. A Soviet *front* directed several armies across a broad theater. The September 14 instructions organized the attack through seven named operational groups, each assigned a commander, formations and objectives. Their concentration-area names are retained below because they describe the commands in those particular orders; subsequent army reorganizations should not be read back into the document. [10] The northern groups were to advance toward Wilno, Grodno and Baranowicze; the southern groups through Volhynia toward Lwów and the Romanian frontier. Both directives told commanders to bypass fortified positions rather than become absorbed in frontal attacks. Screens were to hold defenders in place while the main forces went around their flanks and into their rear. This made resistance at a border post precarious: holding the position could leave its garrison cut off as mobile Soviet forces continued west.

The southern order expected the Shepetovka group to take the Równe–Dubno area by the end of September 17 and Łuck on the 18th. Golikov’s group received successive objectives on the approach to Lwów; Tyulenev’s was to reach the Strypa and then Stanisławów, cutting Polish troops off from Romania. These deadlines show what headquarters demanded, not what every formation achieved. The instructions also ordered continuous supply and forbade unauthorized requisition of food and fodder. The order made supplying the troops a command responsibility; it did not authorize them to help themselves to food in the occupied districts. [9]

Reading the atlas

An arrow can show an intention

Open the September 17 map to see the seven planned directions. The lines are deliberately schematic. Their endpoints identify the direction of later objectives; they do not mean that Soviet troops stood there on the first evening. Front labels identify command sectors, not headquarters. The battles discussed below occurred over the following fortnight and remain dated separately in the campaign chronology.

The Polish decision: fight, withdraw, or preserve the army

Reports of resistance reached foreign capitals almost immediately. On the morning of September 17, Poland’s ambassador in Paris told William Bullitt, the American ambassador, that Soviet troops had entered the northeast and that Polish forces were fighting them. This was a report received through diplomatic channels, not an independently surveyed front line. It nevertheless records Polish units resisting at the outset, before their commanders could absorb the implications of a war on two fronts. [11] Marshal Edward Rydz-Śmigły’s response attempted to preserve what remained of Poland’s armed forces. He directed a general withdrawal toward Romania and Hungary and instructed troops to avoid combat with the Soviets unless attacked or subjected to disarmament. That qualification was crucial. The order was neither an invitation to join the Red Army nor an unconditional instruction to surrender. It sought to prevent an already hard-pressed army from exhausting itself against another vastly superior opponent while routes out of the country might still be available. [2] The qualification left commanders with decisions that a general order could not resolve for them. A demand for disarmament threatened the capacity to continue the war; resistance could close an escape route or expose civilians to further fighting. A withdrawal might preserve soldiers while abandoning a crossing needed by other formations. Grodno, Lwów and the Border Protection Corps would produce different answers because each faced a different combination of military pressure, communication and opportunity. The government’s movement into Romania during the night of September 17–18 came after the Soviet invasion had begun. Its departure therefore cannot explain an attack publicly justified before it happened. Nor did crossing a frontier automatically extinguish the state or the allegiance of its armed forces. The immediate result was nevertheless disastrous for command: leaders attempting to continue their work abroad instead faced internment, while soldiers still inside Poland had to act amid rapidly narrowing options. Poland’s political and military continuation would have to be rebuilt outside the country. [12] Refugees faced the same closing roads. The Holocaust Memorial Museum describes people leaving the German advance with whatever transport they could obtain, often without an agreed destination. Soviet entry made the eastern refuge another occupied territory. Families now had to decide whether to keep moving, cross a foreign frontier or search for relatives in a place that had just changed hands. Those decisions were made without reliable knowledge of what either occupation would become. [13]

Where the advance met resistance

Wilno, now Vilnius, was fought over on **September 18–19**. Grodno resisted on **September 20–22**, with the principal fighting on the first two days and withdrawal continuing into the third. The Red Army’s numerical and material advantage did not remove the need to take defended places. As its columns approached, local commanders had to decide whether their remaining troops could hold the city, cover an evacuation or still get away. [2] Grodno illustrates the weakness concealed by a fast armored approach. Much of its regular garrison had already been sent elsewhere. Major Benedykt Serafin helped organize a defense drawing on remaining servicemen and volunteers. On September 20, tanks of the Soviet 27th Tank Brigade entered across the Niemen bridge without sufficient infantry support. Polish defenders used the weapons available, including gasoline bottles at close range. Tanks inside streets could be attacked from positions their crews had difficulty seeing or reaching. Soviet reinforcements made the struggle increasingly unequal, and the main Polish forces withdrew during the night of September 21–22. [14] The withdrawal led to further fighting near Kodziowce during the night of September 21–22. The Polish 101st Reserve Uhlan Regiment, commanded by Major Stanisław Żukowski, encountered a Soviet mobile detachment associated with the 2nd Tank Brigade. The episode belongs to the history of cavalry operating against armor, but should not be reduced to a contest between a horse and a tank. It was a confused fight involving movement through villages and darkness, with Polish units trying to keep a route toward the Lithuanian frontier open. [15]

A soldier’s field of view

Three kilometers from a battle

Lieutenant Piotr Łazarewicz recorded that his exhausted company slept until seven on September 22, unaware of fighting about three kilometers away. When it moved toward prepared trenches, those defenses faced the Germans. His diary brings the campaign down to the scale of an officer receiving fragments of news, looking for cover and waiting for a messenger. His account of enemy losses came from another officer; it is not an independently checked tally. [12]

Farther south, General Wilhelm Orlik-Rückemann concentrated surviving Border Protection Corps troops into an improvised force. At **Szack on September 28–29**, they broke through Soviet opposition with the help of concealed 37-mm antitank guns. The victory opened a route toward the Bug. It also left fewer men and less equipment for the next fight. Orlik-Rückemann reported exhaustion from prolonged marching and the lack of hot meals; during the subsequent crossing some trucks had to be abandoned and burned, while another element had already lost much of its transport and its antitank platoon. At **Wytyczno on October 1**, the depleted force met renewed Soviet attacks. Colonel Nikodem Sulik judged that his troops could no longer hold their positions, and Orlik-Rückemann ordered withdrawal and dissolved the formation. Soldiers separated into smaller groups to evade pursuit; some later joined General Franciszek Kleeberg’s forces. This was a commanded dispersal under pressure, not evidence of a collective refusal to fight. The same men who had broken through at Szack could no longer sustain their formation through another battle. [16]

Lwów and the value of a promise

Lwów confronted the Soviet advance while already defending itself against Germany. German attempts to seize the city had begun on September 12 and met resistance. On September 18, the armored trains Śmiały and Bartosz Głowacki reached the city; Soviet forward units attacked during the following night and were repulsed. The arrival of Śmiały provides a tangible connection with the first invasion study, where the train supported the fighting at Mokra. Equipment and men were still moving through Poland, even as the space in which they could operate contracted. [17] German forces subsequently withdrew from around Lwów under the arrangements between the occupying powers. For the defenders, that movement did not restore a secure rear or end the siege. It changed the immediate opponent with whom the city’s fate would be negotiated. General Władysław Langner accepted terms on September 22 that promised personal liberty and freedom of movement to Polish officers and protection of civilian property. Soviet authorities then violated those assurances and took Polish servicemen into captivity. [17] The terms offered Langner a means of ending the siege while preserving his officers’ liberty and the population’s property. Their breach must be distinguished from the mere fact that a garrison surrendered. Soldiers who laid down their arms under agreed guarantees had not forfeited those guarantees by accepting them. Soviet forces also killed soldiers and police officers and looted civilian property after entering the city. The military agreement that ended the defense therefore failed to protect the people for whom its conditions mattered most. [17] Soviet troops also killed captured defenders after the fighting at Grodno, and Red Army personnel and the NKVD—the Soviet internal-affairs commissariat and its security police—carried out killings and arrests as occupation spread. Published estimates for particular incidents and for the invasion as a whole vary; no precise campaign-wide killing total can be established from the sources used here. The documented acts remain distinct from deaths in combat. A defender who had been disarmed was a prisoner, even when the occupying authorities treated earlier resistance as a reason to punish him. [18]

Soldiers, civilians and incompatible expectations

Official instructions presented the invasion to Soviet soldiers as liberation from national and class oppression. A political report dated September 13, discussed in an Institute of National Remembrance study, nevertheless recorded confusion among commanders of the 13th Rifle Corps. Its chief of staff asked whether their sympathies should lie with Poland or Germany. That reported question documents uncertainty about the diplomatic reversal; it does not establish refusal to obey orders or a mutiny. Political surveillance preserved remarks selected for official attention, not a representative sample of what every soldier thought. [19]

A changing explanation

Simonov’s remembered reaction

Konstantin Simonov later recalled sympathy for Poland when Germany attacked and then approval of Soviet intervention when it was presented as protection for threatened populations. He was a young correspondent in Mongolia, not an eyewitness to the Polish frontier crossings. His retrospective account is useful as one person’s recollection of how the official explanation could reconcile apparently conflicting feelings. It should not be treated as the voice of every Soviet soldier. [19]

Nor did eastern Poland produce a single response to the invading army. National, religious, class and local attachments could pull in different directions. Stanisław Boridczenko’s research traces sharply different reactions in neighboring communities and examines the assumptions with which Polish officers later described them. Some inhabitants welcomed Soviet troops or attacked Polish institutions; others assisted Polish soldiers, fled, or tried to avoid involvement. A report of violence in one locality cannot establish the conduct of an entire national or religious community. [20] Boridczenko quotes Orlik-Rückemann’s March 1940 report on evacuating military families from Pińsk to Dawidgródek. The general said he had moved them to protect them from local hostility and believed the move had succeeded. This is a commander’s retrospective account, but it records a practical act of protection whose outcome depended on differences between places. Other testimony in the study distinguishes armed attackers from inhabitants who condemned their conduct. Assistance and persecution could occur close together under the same changing occupation. [20] Military service also cut across ethnic assumptions. Boridczenko cites Captain Adam Jarosiński of the 79th Infantry Regiment recalling that his 7th Company, with a high proportion of Belarusians, remained reliable through the campaign and produced no deserters. That recollection concerns one company and cannot establish an army-wide rate. It does challenge the assumption that minority soldiers necessarily deserted as the state lost territory. In the same campaign, units could disintegrate through capture, separation or authorized dispersal; those outcomes need evidence of their own before they can be classified as desertion. [20] Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi persecution could experience the arrival of Soviet troops as an immediate escape from German violence. That did not imply consent to everything Soviet rule imposed. The Museum’s refugee history follows people who stayed, sought another frontier or later returned toward family in German-held territory; some subsequently suffered Soviet arrest and deportation. Those later experiences should not be projected into the refugees’ first decisions. The [boundary-treaty study](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28#life-across-the-boundary) follows the consequences when the route across Poland became a guarded partition frontier. [13]

Foreign obligations, refugees and recognition

Polish diplomacy had no difficulty identifying the Soviet action as aggression. On the evening of September 17, Bullitt reported that Poland’s ambassador in Paris had received Foreign Minister Józef Beck’s denunciation of the invasion. The ambassador also expressed bitter disappointment at the lack of effective British and French help and deep pessimism about Romania’s willingness to act. This was the view from a diplomatic post trying to obtain assistance while the military situation deteriorated faster than allied discussions could change it. [21] In London, the next day’s conversation between American ambassador Joseph Kennedy and senior Foreign Office official Alexander Cadogan revealed a different calculation. Cadogan did not consider Britain automatically at war with the Soviet Union under its agreement with Poland. He said the Polish ambassador had requested a formal protest but had not asked Britain to declare war. The same report records rejection of Moscow’s claim that the Polish government had ceased to exist. British officials could reject the justification while declining to enlarge the war. [22] The terms of the British commitment help explain this response. Although the public Anglo-Polish agreement referred generally to aggression by a European power, its secret protocol defined that power, for the relevant obligation, as Germany. Megan Donaldson’s study of treaty secrecy establishes both the restriction and the fact that the protocol remained unpublished until 1945. Britain was therefore not treating its specific promise against Germany as an automatic declaration of war against every invader of Poland. That explains the scope of the obligation; it does not make the Soviet attack lawful or the British choice politically unavoidable. Cadogan’s conversation shows a government declining to extend an already dangerous war while maintaining that Poland continued to exist. [23] [22] French discussion was already turning to the next phase of the war. Bullitt’s dispatch of **September 20** reported concern about a German offensive in the west, danger to Romania and the long preparation thought necessary for a successful Allied attack. These were contemporary assessments, not reliable forecasts. They help explain why France, already fighting Germany, made no declaration of war against the Soviet Union or immediate attempt to relieve Poland from the east. Poland needed assistance during the remaining campaign; Allied planning increasingly addressed the war expected to follow its defeat. [24] Romania confronted the retreat at its own frontier. An American report of **September 20** recorded German pressure on Bucharest and restrictions on the Polish leadership, including its use of cipher communications. Romania refused to treat the leaders simply as a functioning government passing through to continue its work elsewhere. Internment cut across their plan of evacuation and made succession urgent. The same report described efforts to establish a constitutionally valid successor government in France. This was a crisis in the exercise of Polish authority, not evidence that no Polish state had existed when Soviet troops attacked. [25] Hungary provided another route out. Its authorities interned Polish soldiers but also tolerated assistance to men moving onward to join Polish forces abroad. After Rydz-Śmigły’s withdrawal order, crossing a neutral frontier could be a means of continuing military service, rather than desertion from it. The contrast with Romania concerns the treatment of people seeking passage, not a claim that every refugee enjoyed unrestricted freedom in Hungary. The survival of trained personnel gave evacuation a purpose that extended beyond the loss of their original formations. [26] The United States remained neutral while its diplomats followed the invasion and the displacement of Poland’s government. On **October 2**, Secretary of State Cordell Hull explicitly confirmed continued recognition. The [next study](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28#poland-refuses) examines that diplomatic continuity and Poland’s rejection of partition. For the troops and civilians still inside the country, recognition preserved a claim that foreign governments accepted; it supplied no immediate protection against either occupying army. [27] [28] At Brest on September 22, German and Soviet commanders presided over a military ceremony as the German occupation gave way to Soviet possession. Heinz Guderian and Semyon Krivoshein appeared together there. The occasion made visible the cooperation described in the telegrams: the arrival of the second invading army could be arranged with the first, while the state whose territory they occupied had no voice in the transfer. [29] [28] Cooperation did not settle every territorial question. On **September 19**, Molotov told Schulenburg that Moscow now preferred partition to the earlier possibility of preserving a reduced Polish state. The decision concerned what the occupiers would build after defeating the remaining resistance. While Polish soldiers attempted to escape or negotiated surrender, Berlin and Moscow were moving from operational coordination to a revised political settlement. [30]

The invasion becomes an occupation

The political program had also begun before the frontier crossing. A Byelorussian Front directive dated September 16 instructed officials to create temporary administrations including army and NKVD representatives, organize newspapers and arrange the transfer of landed property. It explicitly postponed the creation of collective farms. This was preparation to replace existing authority and reshape society, with the pace of particular measures adjusted to the immediate situation. The instruction is a useful corrective to the suggestion that administration developed only as an improvised response to disorder after the troops arrived. [12] The directive joined military and political coercion from the beginning. Temporary administrations would accompany the advance, supported by the army and security police, while promises of land redistribution sought support among selected inhabitants. A welcome for a particular policy gave those inhabitants no control over the government imposing it. Officials of the Polish state, police officers and others classified as opponents were already being arrested. The occupation’s institutions were beginning to decide who could hold property, exercise authority or remain free. [12] [18] Capture also led to different kinds of detention. Some rank-and-file prisoners were released in autumn 1939; others were transferred to German custody or put into Soviet forced-labor camps. Officers and police were selected for continued confinement. Those decisions, rather than capture alone, created the routes into the special camps associated with the Katyn murders in spring 1940. The later executions were a subsequent policy and must not be dated to September. They grew from a system of custody that the invasion had made possible. [18] By the beginning of October, the second invasion had destroyed the possibility of using eastern Poland as a secure base for regrouping. Grodno had been taken, Lwów had surrendered under guarantees the Soviet authorities broke, and the Border Protection Corps formation had dispersed after Wytyczno. Some men escaped to continue the war; others entered captivity or remained under occupation. The government’s work would continue abroad, but it could no longer protect people inside the country. The [agreement dated September 28](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28) sought to give the two invasions a lasting political form. Polish military defeat had made that bargain possible; it had not supplied Polish consent.
author: Robert M. Dobo
location: Eastern Poland, Moscow and the European capitals
summary: Moscow presented a prepared offensive as protection for threatened populations. Polish soldiers and civilians confronted shrinking opportunities for resistance, regrouping and escape as Soviet formations advanced from the east.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below, with locators and backlinks. Contemporary Soviet orders are compared with German and American diplomatic reports, Polish military scholarship, museum research and testimony. Published Russian transcriptions were read, but not checked against original manuscript images. Operational orders establish intended objectives and restrictions, not compliance or daily positions. Surrender guarantees, subsequent captivity and killings are distinguished. Later releases, deportations and the Katyn murders are explicitly separated from the invasion. Boridczenko’s local and military accounts are attributed to their witnesses; a recollection about one company is not treated as an army-wide desertion statistic. Reported political uncertainty among Soviet officers is not labeled mutiny. Uncertain casualty totals are omitted.
